issues.legal_issue: The statutory validation of Atiyat orders made during the specified transition period did not violate the guarantee of equality.
material_facts: A succession dispute concerned Atiyat jagir property, and an executive order resolving it was made during the period between the commencement of the political transition and the commencement of the validating legislation.
The legislation validated orders made by specified authorities during that period in all relevant enquiries, rather than validating only the order in this dispute.
Major historical events occurred in the State during that period.
The jagir was not automatically heritable: on the holder’s death it reverted to the State and could be re-granted at the State’s discretion.
The petitioners did not establish that comparable enquiries were left outside the class of validated orders.
issues.conclusion: The challenge under Article 14 failed. The period-based classification was permissible, and the petitioners had no right to have succession to the jagir determined by a civil court as an inheritable claim.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 permits legislation to treat orders made during a historically distinctive period as a separate class where the classification is not shown to be discriminatory. Section 13(2) of the Hyderabad Atiyat Enquiries Act, 1952 validated covered orders generally, not merely the order in this dispute. Unlike the heritable property considered in Ammeerunnissa Begum v. Mahboob Begum, [1953] S.C.R. 404, a jagir was subject to resumption and discretionary re-grant, so a claimant had no civil right of succession to enforce under personal law.

rule.if: constitutional_validity_challenge and transition_period_orders and validation_covers_the_class_generally and historically_distinct_period and jagir_is_not_automatically_inheritable

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A party challenges the validity of a measure that validates prior administrative decisions.
predicates.transition_period_orders: The disputed administrative decision was made during a period of political transition treated by the legislature as significant.
predicates.validation_covers_the_class_generally: The measure validates covered decisions across the relevant class of enquiries, rather than selecting only the decision affecting the challenger.
predicates.historically_distinct_period: Major historical events occurred during the period used to define the class of decisions.
predicates.jagir_is_not_automatically_inheritable: The property reverted to the State on the holder’s death and any successor received it only through a discretionary re-grant.
predicates.validation_survives_equality_review: The validating measure is not invalidated on equality grounds.

issues.definition: When a generally applicable validation measure covers decisions made during a historically distinct period, and the property at issue was not automatically inheritable, the measure survives equality review.

issues.legal_issue: The validation of orders concerning non-heritable jagir property did not violate the constitutional protection of property.
material_facts: The petitioners challenged the validating provision in relation to Atiyat jagir property.
The jagir reverted to the State upon the holder’s death, and a successor obtained it only if the State chose to re-grant it.
The claimed interest was therefore not an automatic right of inheritance in the jagir.
issues.conclusion: The challenge under Article 19(1)(f) failed because of the special legal character of the property.
issues.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(f) did not invalidate the provision in relation to property that was not heritable as of right and could pass to a claimant only through the State’s discretionary re-grant. The Court relied on the legal character of jagir property described in its discussion of the relevant Firmans and Atiyat enquiry arrangements.

predicates.constitutional_property_rights_challenge: A party challenges a measure as infringing a constitutional protection of property.
predicates.proceeding_concerns_jagir_property: The dispute concerns a jagir held subject to the State’s power to resume and re-grant it.
predicates.property_is_not_automatically_inheritabl: The holder’s heirs do not acquire the property automatically on the holder’s death.
predicates.property_rights_challenge_fails: The constitutional property-rights challenge is rejected.

issues.definition: A constitutional property-rights challenge fails when it concerns jagir property that does not pass automatically to heirs.

issues.legal_issue: An order resolving succession to Atiyat property did not determine title to the deceased holder’s non-Atiyat property, which remained triable in civil court.
material_facts: The deceased holder’s estate included both Atiyat and non-Atiyat property.
The order confirming the succession enquiry was broad in wording, but the parties accepted that it did not cover the non-Atiyat property.
A civil suit concerning some of that property was pending.
issues.conclusion: The order did not relate to the non-Atiyat property, and questions of title to that property were to be tried in the civil courts.
issues.legal_principle: The validation of decisions concerning Atiyat grants did not extend the order to non-Atiyat property where the parties accepted that the order did not cover it. Title to the non-Atiyat property remained for determination by the ordinary civil courts.

predicates.succession_scope_dispute: A dispute concerns whether an administrative succession order determines rights in particular estate property.
predicates.estate_contains_non_atiyat_property: The estate includes property that is not an Atiyat grant or jagir.
predicates.parties_accept_order_does_not_cover_that: The parties agree that the succession order does not extend to the non-Atiyat property.
predicates.civil_courts_determine_non_atiyat_title: Title to the non-Atiyat property remains for determination in civil court.

issues.definition: When a succession dispute concerns non-Atiyat property and the parties accept that the order does not cover it, civil courts determine title to that property.
